items.title: Interactive Portfolio
items.shortDescription: A single-page React portfolio with a live WebGL background, GSAP animations, custom cursors, and spatial sound effects.
items.description:
Overview

This portfolio site is a showcase of my work at the intersection of web development and computer graphics. Built with React 19 and Vite, it uses a live WebGL shader for the background, GSAP for scroll animations, and Howler for spatial sound.

Key Features

  • Live WebGL Silk background shader
  • GSAP-powered scroll-triggered animations
  • Custom cursor with hover targeting
  • Spatial sound effects with mute toggle
  • Full-screen detail overlays via react-router-dom
  • Dark theme with glassmorphism cards

Tech Stack

React 19, Vite 6, Tailwind CSS v4, GSAP, ogl/WebGL, Howler

items.title: Spiritual Mantra
items.shortDescription: Winner of LPU Hackathon 2023 — a meditation app delivering ambient soundscapes and personalized mantra recommendations.
items.description:
The Concept

Meditation meets technology. Spiritual Mantra helps users find calm through curated ambient soundscapes and AI-recommended mantras based on mood detection.

Features

  • Real-time mood detection from user input
  • Curated ambient sound library
  • Personalized daily mantra recommendations
  • Progress tracking and streaks

Architecture

Built with a React frontend and Node.js + MongoDB backend. The recommendation engine uses a simple rule-based system that maps moods to mantras, with plans to integrate ML for deeper personalization.

Recognition

Won the Best UI/UX award at LPU Hackathon 2023 out of 80+ teams.

items.title: VisionLab
items.shortDescription: A computer vision toolkit for edge detection, face recognition, and object tracking, built with Python and OpenCV.
items.description:
VisionLab Toolkit

A collection of computer vision utilities that demonstrate core CV techniques — edge detection, feature matching, face recognition, and motion tracking — all built from scratch with Python and OpenCV.

Modules

  • EdgeFlow — Canny edge detection with multi-scale Gaussian pre-filtering for real-time video streams.
  • FaceTrace — Haar cascade face detection combined with a Kalman filter for jitter-free tracking.
  • MotionWatch — Background subtraction and optical flow for motion detection.

Web Integration

The toolkit exposes a Flask API that serves detection results to a React dashboard, creating a full pipeline from camera capture to browser visualization.

items.title: TaskFlow
items.shortDescription: A collaborative task management app with real-time updates, built with React, Node.js, and MongoDB.
items.description:
Real-Time Collaboration

TaskFlow brings teams together with real-time task boards, live cursor presence, and instant notifications. Built as a full-stack JavaScript application from the ground up.

Tech Choices

  • React + Socket.IO — the frontend syncs task updates in real-time across all connected clients.
  • Node.js + MongoDB — event-driven backend with change streams for live updates.
  • Tailwind CSS — utility-first styling with custom dark theme.

Performance

Implemented query optimization with MongoDB indexing on project and user fields. Virtualized task lists handle 500+ items without jank. Redis caching on user profiles cuts response times to under 10ms.

posts.title: Building an Interactive Portfolio with React & WebGL
posts.excerpt: How I built this portfolio site — a single-page React app with a live WebGL background, GSAP-driven animations, custom cursors, and spatial sound effects.
posts.content:
The Spark

Every developer's portfolio is a love letter to their craft. For me, it became a playground to explore the intersection of performance, interactivity, and aesthetics — and to ship something that genuinely reflects how I think about building software.

Tech Stack

  • React 19 + Vite 6 — the foundation. Fast HMR and out-of-the-box ESM.
  • Tailwind CSS v4 — utility-first styling with a dark-theme token system.
  • ogl / WebGL — the Silk background shader, compiled to a single 647 kB chunk.
  • GSAP — scroll-triggered animations, staggered reveals, and smooth transitions.
  • Howler — spatial sound effects (hover, click, navigation) that respect prefers-reduced-motion.

Architecture Decisions

The app is a one-page scroll site with anchor navigation. But project and blog detail views open as immersive full-screen overlays via react-router-dom routes — the home sections stay mounted underneath so closing never triggers a re-mount or flash. This keeps the WebGL background alive and the UX buttery.

The WebGL Background

Silk renders a custom fragment shader that creates a flowing, noise-driven gradient. On mobile (<768px) it's disabled for battery and performance — the CSS gradient fallback takes over. prefers-reduced-motion kills both the shader animation and the custom cursor.

Lessons Learned

  1. Bundle budget is real. The Silk chunk is the biggest offender at 866 kB raw. Lazy-loading it below-the-fold or code-splitting could cut the initial load dramatically.
  2. Graceful fallbacks everywhere. The site works with the entire backend down — content falls back from /api/content to content.json, and the ambient audio falls back to a generated drone tone.
  3. Accessibility first. Respecting prefers-reduced-motion and reducing motion on touch devices wasn't an afterthought — it shaped the component design from day one.

Looking Ahead

The next iteration will tackle code-splitting the Silk background, pruning unused effect libraries, and adding proper ESLint with Prettier for consistent style enforcement. The journey never really ends — but the site ships today.

posts.title: Practical Computer Vision Projects with OpenCV
posts.excerpt: Exploring real-world computer vision applications built with Python and OpenCV — from object detection and edge detection to face recognition and motion tracking.
posts.content:
Why Computer Vision

Computer vision bridges the gap between the digital and physical worlds. As someone who started with web development, diving into CV opened up an entirely new dimension of problem-solving — one where pixels aren't just rendered, they're understood.

Project 1: Real-Time Edge Detection

The classic Canny edge detector is a gateway. But tuning it for real-time video required balancing kernel sizes, thresholds, and frame-rate. The key insight: blur lightly with a Gaussian filter first, then let Canny do its work. The result was a fluid 30 FPS pipeline that could run on a laptop webcam.

Project 2: Face Detection & Tracking

Using Haar cascades for frontal face detection is reliable but slow. For tracking, I implemented a Kalman filter that predicts position between detections — this smoothed jitter and maintained tracking even when the face briefly left the frame. The combination of detection + prediction was far more robust than either alone.

Project 3: Object Detection with YOLO

YOLOv5 (via PyTorch) gave me bounding boxes in real-time. The challenge was optimizing inference — quantizing the model and batching frames brought latency down to ~15ms per frame. I also built a lightweight API wrapper so the model could be consumed by a React frontend.

Lessons

  • Data quality matters more than model choice. Noisy training data will silently tank your precision.
  • Preprocessing is half the pipeline. Color space conversion (BGR ↔ HSV), histogram equalization, and noise reduction often matter more than the algorithm itself.
  • Web integration is the frontier. Running CV in the browser via TensorFlow.js or WebAssembly is increasingly viable for lightweight tasks.

Tech Stack

Python, OpenCV, NumPy, PyTorch, Flask, and a React frontend for dashboards. The full pipeline — from camera capture to result display — runs end-to-end with sub-200ms latency.

posts.title: Full-Stack Performance: Optimizing React + Node APIs
posts.excerpt: A deep dive into practical performance optimization techniques for React frontends and Node.js + MongoDB backends — from database indexing to lazy loading strategies.
posts.content:
The Performance Mindset

Performance isn't a post-launch concern — it's a design constraint. Every millisecond of latency erodes user trust. In full-stack applications, bottlenecks hide in unexpected places: the database query you forgot to index, the component re-rendering unnecessarily, the response payload carrying 50 fields the client doesn't need.

Frontend: React Optimizations

The biggest wins came from:

  • Code-splitting with React.lazy + Suspense. Route-level splitting cut the initial bundle by 60%.
    • Memoization with useMemo and useCallback to prevent expensive recalculations. This is especially critical in list rendering where a single unmemoized function can cascade re-renders through the entire tree.
  • Virtualization for long lists. react-window made rendering hundreds of project cards trivially smooth.

Backend: Node.js + MongoDB

Indexing strategy: Composite indexes on the fields you filter and sort by together. A single db.projects.createIndex({ category: 1, sortOrder: 1 }) turned a 3-second query into 15ms.

Projection: Only select the fields the client needs. Returning full documents with nested arrays when the client needs a title and thumbnail is a common waste.

Connection pooling: Reusing MongoDB connections per request — closing connections after each query created connection storms under load.

Caching Layer

A Redis layer for read-heavy endpoints (project listings, stats) brought 99th-percentile latency from 120ms to <5ms. Cache invalidation is the hard problem — I used a simple TTL + explicit invalidation on writes.

Measuring

Without metrics, you're guessing. Lighthouse for frontend, clinic.js for backend profiling, and custom middleware logging response times. The rule: measure first, optimize second, verify third.

Quick Wins

  1. Enable gzip/brotli on your CDN and server.
  2. Leverage HTTP/2 for multiplexed requests.
  3. Preload critical fonts and above-the-fold images.
  4. Use loading='lazy' on everything below the fold.
